findings.title: Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response
findings.body: The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP/Kubernetes request contexts are cancelled when the handler returns, which happens immediately after the unified-storage write response is returned. Consequently the goroutine will commonly invoke Legacy.Create with an already-cancelled context (and the same applies to Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection), so the intended legacy safety copy is silently skipped or aborted. Create a detached context (for example, context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) before applying the bounded timeout, while preserving needed request metadata.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes can be applied out of unified-storage order
findings.body: Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. Unified storage can commit a create followed by an update/delete, while their legacy goroutines run in the opposite order: an update may fail because the create has not reached legacy yet, or a delayed create may recreate stale data after a successful legacy delete. This leaves the legacy store divergent despite both operations succeeding in unified storage. Legacy replication needs an ordered per-resource queue/retry mechanism (including handling failed predecessors), rather than one unconstrained goroutine per request.

findings.title: Every write can retain an unbounded goroutine for ten seconds
findings.body: A goroutine is spawned for every successful write and may remain blocked in a legacy storage call until the ten-second timeout. There is no concurrency limit, queue bound, or backpressure, so a legacy outage combined with normal or burst write traffic accumulates arbitrarily many goroutines and pending request objects, risking memory/resource exhaustion. Use a bounded worker queue or concurrency limiter and define behavior when it is full.

findings.title: Mode 3 records several storage outcomes against the wrong metrics
findings.body: When Create or Update fails in unified storage, the code calls recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129) instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified failures are reported as legacy failures. Additionally, successful Delete uses the object name as the kind label (line 106), and the asynchronous DeleteCollection legacy operation calls recordStorageDuration (line 166). These produce misleading duration/error metrics and high-cardinality labels, preventing operators from reliably detecting which backend is failing.
